idiom_name: final-by-default members: public entry point (no modifier) + open/abstract hooks
implementation_notes: Kotlin's inheritance rules are the pattern: classes and their members are final unless marked `open` (abstract members are implicitly open), and an overriding member must say `override` - so a public function written with no modifier is already non-overridable, and the customisation point is the member deliberately marked `protected open` or declared abstract. There is nothing to emulate, which makes Kotlin a native fit; keep the wrapper out of interfaces, whose members are open by default. Add `final` to an `override` when a subclass implementation must not be overridden further.
pitfalls: Marking the wrapper `open`, or putting it in an interface (members are open by default), silently re-opens the contract.
An inherited `override` member is itself open; add `final` to stop further overriding.
A `public` hook lets clients bypass the wrapper - hooks should stay `protected` (or `internal`) unless there is a reason to expose them.
